section: Strike Zone Whiff Rate: Mike Trout (Pre- vs. Post-Statcast MVP)
text:
Strike Zone Whiff Rate: Mike Trout (Pre- vs. Post-Statcast MVP)
The evolution between Mike Trout’s 2014 and 2019 strike zones illustrates how tracking technology created a data-driven arms race between hitters and pitchers. In the early Statcast era, teams utilized high-speed optical cameras and radar to measure pitch spin rates and induced vertical break, discovering that elevated fastballs were uniquely effective at generating whiffs against modern uppercut swing paths. Concurrently, hitters used granular pitch-tracking feedback and video analytics to eliminate swing inefficiencies, allowing Trout to virtually master the middle of the plate—his whiff rate in the heart of the zone dropped from 12.2% in 2014 down to just 4.9% in 2019. In response, pitchers adjusted their scouting heat maps away from the center and attacked the upper quadrant with high-spin velocity, elevating his whiff rate at the top of the zone to 23.0%. This shift demonstrates the broader impact of Statcast: as tracking data helped elite hitters dominate hittable pitches, pitchers adapted by targeting the extreme vertical boundaries of the strike zone.









Between 2014 and 2019, Trout virtually eliminated whiffs in the heart of the zone—dropping from a 12.2% whiff rate down to 4.9%. Concurrently, pitchers shifted to attacking him with high fastballs, where his swing-and-miss rate increased to 23% in the upper-inside quadrant.

title: Story
text: I have played baseball since I was young and am on the baseball team here at New College. As an athlete it is hard not to think about the statistical part of the game you are a part of, so naturally I was curious about how stats have changed over time in the biggest stage of baseball. I know that now more than ever, technology is a big part of sports, especially in MLB. On top of my curiosity, there has been discourse about this new technology in the baseball community. Many older, more traditional people around baseball do not see a need for technology. They played without it or coached without it, meaning they know they can be efficient without it. Younger, more statistical and analytical people around the game think the opposite, that if technology is not being used, you are missing out. I wanted to see how truly effective this technology was in terms of statistics. In my research, I found a website that lists the individual statistics for each player-season for the last 150 years or so (Lahman’s database). It allowed me to compare certain statistical categories that have improved over the last ten years and then relate them to the introduction of technology. I found that K/9 and Hard Hit % both increased dramatically after the introduction of technology into the game of baseball. This is important because it shows that the technology really has worked for most of the players in the big leagues, whether they were a hitter or pitcher. While there are obviously some outliers, there is an obvious increase in the averages of these stats over the two eras (PreStatCast and PostStatCast). We can see from these statistics that technology has had a positive impact on two very important stats in today’s game, showing that the younger and newer generation of baseball society is being supported by the numbers.

title: Baseball Analysis
text:
The introduction of Major League Baseball’s Statcast system in 2015 revolutionized how the sport is measured and played. By deploying high-resolution cameras and radar across every ballpark, Statcast enabled the tracking of granular metrics like exit velocity, launch angle, and pitch spin rates on every play.
This project examines how key baseball statistics evolved alongside this technological shift. By comparing trends across the pre-Statcast era (2005–2014) and post-Statcast era (2015–2025), we analyze whether the availability of tracking data coincided with noticeable changes in pitching strikeout rates (K/9) and hitter hard-hit percentages.

title: Baseball Analysis
text:
Strikeout Rates Over Time
Each point represents an individual pitcher-season (minimum 30 IP), displaying real pitcher-level variation across thousands of observations. The solid line and points trace the annual league average K/9 across the pre-Statcast and post-Statcast eras.






Between the pre-Statcast era (2005–2014) and the post-Statcast era (2015–2025), average pitcher strikeout rates increased from 7.21 to 8.63 K/9, representing a 19.7% increase across eras (and a 31.5% increase from 6.55 in 2005 to 8.61 in 2025).

title: Baseball Analysis
text:
Hard Hit Rate Over Time
Each point represents a qualifying hitter’s individual hard-hit rate for that season, showing real individual-level variation across 4,251 player-seasons. The solid line and points trace the annual league average across the pre-Statcast era (BIS video-scouted Hard%) and the Statcast era (radar-measured exit velocity ≥ 95 mph).






Average hard-hit rates rose from 30.5% in the pre-Statcast era to 38.5% in the Statcast era—a 26.2% relative increase (an 8.0 percentage-point gain, climbing to 42.1% by 2025). Note that part of this shift coincides with the change in data measurement (scout observation vs. automated radar tracking).
